title: Are there AI-driven R&D tax credit platforms?
description: AI-driven R&D tax credit platforms such as Neo.Tax, TaxRobot and Boast populate Form 6765 from payroll and project data, but need a qualified reviewer.
summary: Yes, AI-driven R&D tax credit platforms, such as Neo.Tax, TaxRobot, Boast and PwC's AI-enhanced services, help U.S. businesses claim the federal research credit under IRC §41 by extracting payroll and project data and populating Form 6765. The key takeaway: use them as an early filter and data engine, with a qualified reviewer making final eligibility decisions.

body.text: Yes, AI-driven R&D tax credit platforms, such as Neo.Tax, TaxRobot, Boast and PwC's AI-enhanced services, help U.S. businesses claim the federal research credit under IRC §41 by extracting payroll and project data and populating Form 6765. The key takeaway: use them as an early filter and data engine, with a qualified reviewer making final eligibility decisions.
Jurisdiction: United States (federal research credit under Internal Revenue Code §41). Text labeled "Analysis" is interpretation, not a statement of law.
1. Short answer

Yes. AI-driven and automation-based platforms for the U.S. research credit under IRC §41 are on the market and in use. Examples include Neo.Tax (offered inside Thomson Reuters ONESOURCE), TaxRobot, Boast, and AI-enhanced service lines at large advisers such as PwC. Most of these offerings pair software with human specialists rather than relying on software alone, so the market is best described as a spectrum running from largely self-service software to adviser-led studies that use AI internally.

The statutory tests and the court decisions discussed below support the narrower point that research credit claims fail when documentation does not tie specific activities and costs to the statutory tests. None of the cited court cases involved an AI platform; they involved documentation prepared or assembled by people.
2. AI-driven R&D tax credit platforms: examples

All capability statements in this table are the providers' own descriptions or a vendor-published review. They have not been independently tested, and none of them is an IRS endorsement; the IRS does not certify or approve research credit software.

headers: What the provider says it does

cells: Connects payroll, project management and accounting systems via API to identify qualified research expenses (QREs) and populates Form 6765 in ONESOURCE Income Tax. Says filing time falls "from weeks to days" and that integrations can remove the need for time surveys and technical interviews. Cites over 200 hours a year spent on interviews and up to 150 hours saved.
Vendor statement; the article does not say how the hour figures were measured

"AI-enhanced R&D credits built on software management system data," drawing on systems such as Jira, GitHub and Azure DevOps; specialists use AI-enhanced documentation processes to produce "exam-ready" deliverables.

Describes a hybrid model, "Technology enabled, expert optimized": the platform collects and processes data, and experts identify qualifying activities, optimize federal and state claims and prepare audit-ready documentation.

Describes its software as powered by AI, with linked systems, audit support and value-based pricing (no fee if no credit). Its review also lists Neotax, MainStreet, Clarus R+D, Kipsi, Pilot, KBKG and GOAT Tax, and says R&D software can produce documentation "often in hours, not weeks."
Vendor-published ranking; the review does not attribute AI features to most of the other listed tools

body.text: Analysis: Because the same providers sell both models, the practical question for a U.S. taxpayer is not whether to use "AI" or "a human," but which steps of the §41 analysis are performed by software, which are reviewed by a qualified person, and whether the resulting file can support the business-component reporting and substantiation the IRS now expects. The table above shows that providers themselves describe the software as handling data capture and calculation and describe people as handling qualification and audit readiness.
3. What the platforms are used for

items: MASSIE R&D Tax Credits (November 25, 2025) says AI can scan engineering design documents, JIRA tickets, activity logs and project descriptions at scale and flag possible R&D signals for human review. It also says AI cannot make qualification decisions and that teams treating AI "as an early filter, not a final decision-maker" get the best results.
Thomson Reuters and Neo.Tax describe pulling data from payroll, project management and accounting systems through APIs and populating Form 6765 (see the table above).

PwC describes drawing on software development management systems such as Jira, GitHub and Azure DevOps, which is the kind of contemporaneous project record that maps naturally to a business component.

body.text: Form 6765 Section G and platform data capture. The IRS's Instructions for Form 6765 (revised December 2025) state that Section G, Business Component Information, is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and is required, subject to its own guidelines, for tax years beginning after 2025. The IRS had announced in IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025) that Section G would remain optional for tax year 2025. Practitioner summaries report that filers required to complete Section G must report business components accounting for at least 80 percent of total QREs, up to a cap of 50 business components, and that qualified small businesses electing the reduced payroll tax credit are among those for whom Section G remains optional. Analysis: Section G pushes the return itself toward activity-level, component-level detail.
4. The legal tests any platform has to apply
4.1 The statute (law in force: 26 U.S.C. §41, as amended through Pub. L. 119-21 of July 4, 2025)

That is common practitioner and government shorthand (the United States' own Kyocera brief uses it: the §174 test, the technological information test, the business component test and the process of experimentation test). The statute itself, in §41(d)(1), defines qualified research through three requirements plus an exclusion:

items: (A) the expenditures must be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A (before Pub. L. 119-21 this referred to specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174);
(B) the research must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature and intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component;
(C) substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a permitted purpose; and
the research must not be an activity listed in §41(d)(4).

body.text: The §41(d)(4) exclusions include research after commercial production, adaptation of existing business components, duplication of an existing business component, surveys and studies, certain internal-use computer software, foreign research, social sciences and funded research.

Analysis: Because §41(d)(1)(A) now refers to §174A, a platform that computes QREs must also track whether each cost is a domestic research or experimental expenditure under §174A. Foreign research costs, which remain under §174, are both excluded from QREs by §41(d)(4) and treated differently for deduction purposes. A platform that pulls payroll by location is well placed to make that split; one that does not cannot reliably apply the amended statute.
4.2 The regulations

cells: Satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in §41(d)(3).

The requirements are applied first at the level of the discrete business component; if they are not met there, they apply to the most significant subset of elements. The rule is not itself a reason to exclude research activities.

Immediate (first-line) supervision of qualified research. It does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist.

Services in direct support of persons conducting, or directly supervising, qualified research. It does not include general administrative services or other services only indirectly of benefit to research.

body.text: Hypothetical example (substantially all test). A company spends $500,000 on research activities for one business component, of which $420,000 relates to activities that are elements of a process of experimentation. $420,000 ÷ $500,000 = 0.84, or 84 percent, which meets the 80 percent threshold in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6). If the figure were $380,000, the ratio would be 76 percent, the business component would fail, and the shrinking-back rule would move the analysis to the most significant subset of elements. A platform can do this arithmetic; the classification of each activity feeding it is the judgment step.

Analysis: The shrinking-back rule only helps a taxpayer whose records are kept at a level below the whole product. A platform that ingests tickets, commits or sub-project codes can produce that lower-level breakdown; a platform that only allocates annual wages by department cannot. This is the specific failure discussed in Little Sandy Coal (Section 6.2).
4.3 AI development work and the tests

That list comes from practitioner commentary (MASSIE, July 25, 2025), not from IRS guidance located in this review. MASSIE lists as non-qualifying: using out-of-the-box generative AI tools, automating tasks with pre-trained models with no underlying development, and integrating third-party AI solutions without modification. It advises documenting why existing tools were insufficient.

Analysis: The commentary is consistent with the statutory exclusions for adaptation and duplication of existing business components in §41(d)(4)(B) and (C), but no court decision or IRS publication applying those exclusions to generative AI tools was reviewed here.
5. Limits of automation
These points are practitioner commentary, not law.

items: Interviews and context. DST Advisory Group (June 19, 2025) says AI cannot conduct staff interviews or site visits and handles judgment-heavy tests, such as separating research from routine quality control, poorly.
Data quality. The same article says AI output depends on its inputs and that misallocated wages between qualified and non-qualified work can understate or overstate the credit.

Generic narratives. Tax Cloud (September 19, 2025) warns that AI-written reports can read like marketing copy built on phrases such as "innovative solutions" and "cutting-edge technology," and that template-like reports are easily spotted and rejected. This commentary concerns the UK regime administered by HMRC, not the IRS.

Frontier of knowledge. Alexander Clifford, a UK adviser, argues that AI "does not truly understand the frontier of knowledge." The same article reports that in Elsbury v The Information Commissioner [2025] UKFTT 915 (GRC), the First-tier Tribunal required HMRC to disclose, under the Freedom of Information Act, whether it used AI in handling an R&D claim. This is a UK matter reported by a secondary source; the decision itself was not opened, and it has no bearing on U.S. law.

body.text: The figure is Thomson Reuters' vendor statement of over 200 hours a year, without a stated method.

Analysis: Of the four limits listed, only the data-quality and interview points come from U.S. commentary. The generic-narrative and frontier-of-knowledge points come from the UK and should be read as general cautions rather than descriptions of IRS practice. The U.S. analogue to the generic-narrative concern is the IRS's insistence, reflected in the Form 6765 instructions and the court cases below, on business-component-level facts rather than summary descriptions.
6. Court cases
None of these cases concerned an AI platform.
6.1 Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States

items: Court and case number: U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, Greenville Division, No. 6:22-cv-02440.

From the government's motion for partial summary judgment (filed July 19, 2024): the tax year ended March 31, 2018; the original §41 credit claimed (on a return filed on extension in January 2019) was $398,985; the amended credit (filed July 2021) was $1,709,147, based on employee wages of $23,186,512, supplies of $1,460,503 and contract research of $320,031; Kyocera sought a refund of the unpaid portion, $1,310,162. PwC, retained in August 2019, interviewed 36 employees, and the study covered more than 1,200 employees. The government said Kyocera had no centralized time-tracking system and generally did not track time on the projects at issue, and argued that because Kyocera and PwC failed to create or retain the appropriate documents, the court should rule as a matter of law that the credit could not be substantiated.

In the litigation it was the United States, through the Department of Justice, that argued in federal court that the claim could not be substantiated. No ruling on that motion was located in this review.

Later procedural history: Bloomberg Tax and Law360 reported on March 24, 2025 that Kyocera told the U.S. Tax Court the IRS had incorrectly asserted a new deficiency of about $2.3 million for its fiscal 2018 year, citing a notice of disallowance received at the end of 2024, and that Kyocera argued the burden of proof on that amount was the IRS's. Law360 reported on April 2, 2025 that the South Carolina federal court ruled the Tax Court holds jurisdiction over the overlapping refund dispute (reported at about $7 million). A practitioner summary published in 2026 describes the matter as still pending in the Tax Court. No Tax Court decision was located.

$13.36 million counterclaim: Boast (August 19, 2025) reports that the government countersued, asserting that a $13.36 million 2018 refund was issued in error and demanding repayment plus interest. No court filing confirming this figure was opened, and it differs from the roughly $2.3 million deficiency reported by Bloomberg Tax and Law360.

body.text: 6.2 Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner

items: Citation: 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), No. 21-3145, decided March 7, 2023 (Brennan, J.), affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15.

Holding: the taxpayer failed to prove that substantially all (80 percent or more) of its research activities for the vessels at issue were elements of a process of experimentation, so none of the expenses were QREs. The court said "Just making a prototype model is not enough" and rejected novelty as a shortcut.
Shrinking-back rule: because the taxpayer took an "all or nothing" approach at the whole-vessel level and did not document subcomponents, the courts could not apply the shrinking-back rule.

Business component: The point is narrower: the taxpayer did not break out nonproduction wages by vessel, which blocked the analysis at the business-component level. The Seventh Circuit also held that direct support and supervision activities belong in the substantially-all fraction.

body.text: 6.3 Moore v. Commissioner

items: Citation: T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (February 23, 2023, Colvin, J., Dkt. No. 18632-19), affirmed, 101 F.4th 509 (7th Cir. 2024), No. 23-2681, argued March 27, 2024 and decided April 30, 2024 (Easterbrook, J., for a panel with Jackson-Akiwumi and Lee, JJ.).

Facts and holding: the taxpayers' S corporation, Nevco, Inc., a maker of scoreboards and other sports-venue equipment, treated 65 percent of its president and COO's wages as QREs for 2014 and 2015. The Tax Court found the record did not show what fraction of his time went to qualified research and that he did not provide direct supervision or direct support. The Seventh Circuit affirmed, treating the Tax Court's ruling as a case-specific finding of fact and emphasizing that the COO kept no time records and could not estimate, even approximately, his qualified time.

Neither phrase appears in the decisions or regulations reviewed. The governing rule is Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2): direct supervision means first-line supervision and excludes higher-level managers to whom first-line managers report. RSM's summary (February 27, 2023) states that the COO's supervision was of first-line supervisors and that 65 percent of his salary and bonuses was claimed.

body.text: 6.4 Subsequent documentation decision noted for context

In George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, the Tax Court reviewed seven poultry research trials and held that four constituted qualified research in whole or in part, with the outcome turning largely on the quality of contemporaneous documentation; because base-period records were inadequate, the court did not estimate base-period QREs under the Cohan rule and applied the statutory 6 percent rate. Like the cases above, George did not involve an AI platform. Analysis: It shows that the Tax Court will sort a claim activity by activity, allowing the parts that are documented, which is the kind of granular record a well-configured platform could help preserve.
7. Audit exposure and the IRS position on AI

items: Audit triggers. Aprio (October 3, 2022) states that claiming the credit does not automatically trigger an audit and lists factors that can raise the likelihood, including unusually high credit amounts, refund claims on amended returns, operating in an industry the IRS is focusing on, random or statistical selection, and beginning to use credits after a period of net operating losses. This is practitioner commentary.

Refund-claim and form requirements. For amended-return refund claims, the IRS requires the information set out in the Form 6765 instructions under "Research Credit Claims on Amended Returns," and in IR-2025-99 it extended the transition period for those refund-claim requirements. For original returns, the business-component reporting in Section G becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, as described in Section 3. These are filing requirements, not audit triggers, but they determine what any platform must be able to produce.
IRS warnings about AI. The article's statement that the IRS may demand repayment plus penalties if AI misapplies credits is general commentary.

body.text: 8. Accountability and audit defense

items: Taxpayer liability. The Nasdaq/Zacks article states that the taxpayer, not the software, bears penalties for AI errors. This is commentary; no statute was cited for it. Analysis: As a general matter of U.S. federal tax procedure, the taxpayer signs the return and is the party against whom deficiencies and accuracy-related penalties are assessed; in George, for example, penalties were at issue against the taxpayer and were waived. Whether a software contract shifts any of that cost to a vendor depends on the contract and was not reviewed.

Claims against advisers. Field Seymour Parkes (February 12, 2025) says a client can likely recover damages from an adviser whose R&D advice falls below the standard of a reasonably competent tax adviser, and that a professional indemnity insurer will likely pay a successful claim within the policy's terms. This describes the law of England and Wales, not U.S. law.
Audit defense offerings. Platform and service providers both advertise audit support.

body.text: 9. Legislative update: §174 amortization

That rule has changed. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, added §174A, which allows domestic research or experimental expenditures to be deducted currently (or, by election, capitalized and amortized over not less than 60 months) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. Foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under §174. The Act also amended §280C(c)(1) so that domestic research or experimental expenditures deducted or capitalized under §174A are reduced by the amount of the §41 credit, unless the taxpayer makes the reduced-credit election under §280C(c)(2), which reduces the credit by the maximum corporate rate (21 percent) instead. Transition rules allow unamortized domestic expenditures from tax years beginning in 2022 through 2024 to be deducted in full in the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024 or ratably over two years.

Small business transition relief. Taxpayers meeting the §448(c) gross receipts test (reported as average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the relevant three-year period) may elect to apply §174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 sets out the procedures, including the small business retroactivity election, and a retroactive approach also requires applying the amended §280C(c) for those years, including a one-time window to make or revoke the reduced-credit election on amended returns.

Analysis: For platforms, the relevant capability is no longer handling five-year amortization schedules but correctly coordinating the §41 credit with §174A deductions and §280C elections across amended and current-year returns.
11. Analysis: what the facts mean for the question

AI-driven R&D tax credit platforms exist and are offered both by software companies and by established advisers. Their documented strengths are data extraction from payroll, accounting and engineering systems, population of Form 6765, and flagging of candidate projects. The legal tests in §41(d) and the regulations turn on activity-level facts: whether each activity is part of a process of experimentation, how costs are allocated, whether the costs are domestic research or experimental expenditures under §174A, and who directly supervised the work. Little Sandy Coal, Moore, George and the Kyocera filings show claims failing, in whole or in part, on exactly those points, though in each case the documentation was prepared by people, not software.

Mandatory Section G reporting for tax years beginning after 2025 requires business-component detail on the return itself, and the §174A amendment adds a classification step to every QRE. Both raise the value of platforms that capture contemporaneous project-level data, and both raise the cost of misclassification that a platform cannot detect on its own. The material therefore supports using platforms as an early filter and data engine, with a qualified reviewer making the final eligibility, allocation and election decisions.
